summary: Kole Jain redesigns the Google Gemini landing page from scratch, narrating each section and the choices behind it. He starts from inspiration (Microsoft Copilot, OpenAI, Google Chrome and other Google products), picks a visual recipe of mesh gradients, noise and fully rounded corners, and merges three separate Google landing pages into one. Along the way he shows concrete moves: a typeable search bar instead of a plain button as the hero call to action, a bento section, a gradient trick for adding color to dark mode, hover effects that blur, enlarge and reveal text on image cards, and a privacy section. He also shows iteration openly, walking through about four call-to-action layouts before one felt right, and avoids reusing the same layout twice on one page. For a design system, it gives a worked example of a marketing-page process and of where gradients, hover states and icon choices sit in an AI product's visual language.
key_ideas: Start a redesign by collecting inspiration from competitors and sibling products, then borrow and adapt layouts.
Mesh gradients are called pretty much synonymous with AI; the redesign pairs them with a healthy dose of noise and fully rounded corners.
A typeable search bar as the hero call to action gets the visitor into an action, which the author says makes them more likely to follow through.
Replace decorative background shapes with a product-native animation, such as the chatbot's thinking loader, when the brand style is clean.
Merge redundant landing pages that sell the same thing into one page built around a few key points.
Add color to a dark mode by using a darkened two-color gradient of the primary colors as the background, optionally with some noise, but not so much the site looks like TV static.
Image cards can reveal more on hover by blurring the image, enlarging it and popping up extra text.
Hide options that matter to few visitors (Enterprise) behind a small button on each plan instead of giving them a section.
A good layout carries the design before any animation is added.
Iterate through several layouts for a key section; the final CTA came after about four attempts.
Do not reuse the same layout for two sections of one page.
Products that handle user data need a privacy section, and icon metaphors should match the brand (shield vs lock).
When the hero search bar works, reuse it in the final call to action, with decorative prompt cards moved to the sides.
For clean, simple icons, search Flaticon by interface icons.

topics.name: Landing pages
topics.summary: A full section-by-section landing page redesign for an AI product: search-bar hero, bento features, image showcase, merged pricing/plans, explore section, privacy, CTA, blog and footer.

topics.name: Design process
topics.summary: Gather inspiration first, plan a page roadmap, borrow and adapt layouts, iterate openly (about four CTA layouts), and search for assets before starting.

topics.name: Color
topics.summary: Uses mesh gradients, gradient strokes and a Google blue instead of gradient icons; tried Google's brand colors on the headline and found they looked off.

topics.name: Dark mode and themes
topics.summary: To bring color into dark mode, set the background to a gradient of two primary colors (baby blue and pink) and darken them, optionally with a little noise.

topics.name: Cards and sections
topics.summary: Bento cards with headers, descriptions and integrated diagrams; a plans section where the purchase CTA is one of the cards with a gradient stroke.

topics.name: Micro-interactions
topics.summary: Hover effects: blur the image, enlarge it and reveal extra text (from the Accenture site); a gradient stroke on hover; a zoom-in effect on the Chrome site inspired making the plans section depend on hover.

topics.name: Buttons and actions
topics.summary: A typeable search bar replaces a plain button as the hero CTA and is echoed in the final CTA; the Enterprise option becomes a tiny button on each plan.

topics.name: Icons and imagery
topics.summary: Swaps gradient icons for solid Google blue, picks a shield over a lock to feel like Google, and recommends Flaticon's interface icons for clean icons.

topics.name: Spacing and layout
topics.summary: Shows how much a good layout does before animation, uses a layout that breaks the box by extending off the page, and avoids repeating a layout on one page.

topics.name: Shape and corner radius
topics.summary: Fully rounded corners are part of the chosen AI visual recipe.

topics.name: Design taste and judgement
topics.summary: Critiques AI company sites (lopsided layouts, too many tabs, tiny text, redundant pages) and rejects ideas that look messy or lame against the brand's clean style.

topics.name: Content and microcopy
topics.summary: Writes a punchy headline in the style of the Chrome site and plays on 'unparalleled privacy' with two non-parallel lines.

topics.name: Design resources
topics.summary: Flaticon, filtered to interface icons, as a source of clean simple icons.

topics.name: Paywalls and pricing pages
topics.summary: Merges two paid-tier landing pages into one plans section built on three points (cost, a better AI, document uploads), makes the purchase CTA one of the cards with a gradient stroke, and puts Enterprise behind a tiny button on every plan.

topics.name: AI-assisted design
topics.summary: The page roadmap was partly generated with Gemini and Gemini generated the explore-section content, while the bento card descriptions were written without AI.

rules.rule: Collect inspiration from competitors and sibling products, and search for existing assets, before you start designing.
rules.why: As with any good project you need inspiration, and a Google search turned up a way better background image than the one first planned.
rules.evidence: as with any good project we're going to need some inspiration; that is why you do a Google search before you start a project

rules.rule: On an AI product landing page, use a search or prompt bar the visitor can type into as the hero call to action instead of a plain button.
rules.why: The search bar redirects to log in, but the user is already engaged in an action and is more likely to see it through; it also looks cooler than a plain button.
rules.evidence: open AI has the right idea to have a search bar that you can type in

rules.rule: When a clean hero needs more attention, add a product-native animation (such as the chatbot's thinking loader) rather than decorative background shapes.
rules.why: Background shapes looked messy against the brand's clean style, while the loader makes it look like the AI is actually thinking and is eye-catching.
rules.evidence: integrate the chatbot loading screen into the bottom of the header

rules.rule: Merge landing pages that sell the same thing into one page built around the few key points they share.
rules.why: The author hates redundant landing pages; the two paid-tier pages look like they sell exactly the same thing and reduce to three key points: the cost, a better AI, and uploading Google Docs, Sheets and PDFs.
rules.evidence: there's one thing I hate it's redundant landing pages so let's simplify

rules.rule: To bring color into a dark mode, set the background to a gradient of two primary colors and darken both.
rules.why: It is a trick for when you are struggling to incorporate color into dark modes.
rules.evidence: if you're struggling to incorporate color into your dark modes set your background to a gradient

rules.rule: Use noise on gradients sparingly; do not apply it across the whole site.
rules.why: Too much noise makes the site look like TV static.
rules.evidence: I don't want our whole site to end up looking like TV static

rules.rule: Do not put a section title above a bento grid when it feels redundant; let the card headers carry the section.
rules.why: The planned title seemed kind of redundant, and the cards got their own headers.
rules.evidence: originally I was thinking of having this title up here but it seems kind of redundant

rules.rule: Put the found background image under the card and add a duplicate with a bit of background blur to give the card ambiance.
rules.why: The blurred duplicate gives some ambiance, and the author says the result looks really good.
rules.evidence: add a bit of background blur to a duplicate to give it some Ambiance

rules.rule: Make a section work through layout alone; it should already look good before any animation is added.
rules.why: The page already looked good before any animation, which shows how powerful a good layout is.
rules.evidence: this is before any fancy animations

rules.rule: On hover over an image card, blur the image, make it larger and pop up additional text.
rules.why: The author calls it a really classy interactive effect (seen on the Accenture website) and it lets the section hold more information.
rules.evidence: on Hover we blur the image make it larger and pop up some additional text

rules.rule: Put the purchase call to action inside the row of plan cards as one of the cards, marked with a gradient stroke, instead of placing it above them.
rules.why: It keeps the section more interesting.
rules.evidence: instead of popping the CTA to purchase Gemini Advanced up here let's make it one of these cards

rules.rule: Move an option that only a small share of visitors need (such as Enterprise) into a small button on each plan instead of giving it its own section.
rules.why: The Enterprise part is not useful for most people passing through.
rules.evidence: let's add this tiny button to all the plans

rules.rule: Use a solid brand color for feature icons rather than gradient icons, and add brand color through a gradient stroke on hover.
rules.why: The author did not like the gradient icons; the hover stroke adds color instead.
rules.evidence: grab some gradient icons but I don't like that very much so let's switch that to a nice Google blue

rules.rule: When you cannot find good icons, search Flaticon filtered to interface icons.
rules.why: That filter returns only the clean, simple icons.
rules.evidence: Pro tip if you can't find any good icons for your projects go to Flat icon

rules.rule: Include a privacy section on the landing page of any software or hardware that handles user data.
rules.why: Products that deal with your data need one; Apple devotes an entire page to it.
rules.evidence: for any software or Hardware dealing with your data you need a privacy section

rules.rule: Choose icon metaphors that match the brand's own conventions (a shield felt like Google, a lock like Apple).
rules.why: The shield seems more like Google, whereas Apple generally uses the lock icon.
rules.evidence: I was thinking about using a lock icon but the shield seems more like Google

rules.rule: Try several layouts for a key section like the final CTA, and keep changing it until it feels right.
rules.why: The CTA went through about four layouts (one felt weird, one's spacing was not right, one still did not feel right) before one worked; that is how you iterate to the best design.
rules.evidence: I went through about four different layouts before arriving on one I liked

rules.rule: Do not reuse the same layout for two sections of one page; pick a different layout for the later section.
rules.why: The Microsoft-style blog layout was not a bad option, but the author had already used that layout for the explore section, so he picked another.
rules.evidence: we've kind of already used this layout though for the explore the possibilities section

rules.rule: Do not use tiny text in content sections such as a blog list.
rules.why: The author calls out the tiny text on Microsoft's blog section as a flaw.
rules.evidence: whatever the hell is going on with this tiny text Microsoft

rules.rule: For an AI product's visual style, pair mesh gradients with a healthy dose of noise and fully rounded corners.
rules.why: Mesh gradients are pretty much synonymous with AI at this point.
rules.evidence: mesh gradients are pretty much synonymous with AI

rules.rule: Write a short, punchy hero headline (here 'Gemini, the only AI by Google').
rules.why: The author takes the punchy-headline style from the Chrome website and likes how it sounds.
rules.evidence: steal some inspiration of a Punchy headline from the Chrome website

rules.rule: If brand colors applied to headline text look off, bring in the brand through its logo on a white background instead.
rules.why: Applying the Google colors made something look off.
rules.evidence: I was thinking of applying the Google colors but when I do that something looks off

rules.rule: Build diagrams or real product UI into bento cards instead of leaving them as plain text cards.
rules.why: Integrating the diagrams into the cards felt so Google-esque the author did not think he could do much better; two cards reuse Gemini UI with small changes.
rules.evidence: integrating these diagrams into the cards seems so Google esque

rules.rule: Choose a section layout that leaves room for all the content you need, and drop one that does not, even if it looks good.
rules.why: The first image-section layout was good but did not leave enough room for all the content the author wanted.
rules.evidence: it didn't really leave me enough room to fit in all the content

rules.rule: Add a few real product elements to a showcase so it reads as the actual product (here, chatbot elements around the generated images).
rules.why: To make it feel more like an actual chatbot.
rules.evidence: I added a couple more elements to make it feel more like an actual chatbot

rules.rule: For an explore or browse section, use a layout that breaks the box by letting items extend off the page, with navigation to move through them.
rules.why: It keeps the section simple and is one of the author's favorite layouts.
rules.evidence: breaks the Box by extending off the page

rules.rule: Reuse the hero's typeable search bar as the basis of the final call-to-action section.
rules.why: The CTA needs something eye-catching that draws the user in, and the author says the header search bar nailed that.
rules.evidence: I think we nailed it in the header by having a search bar

rules.rule: In a centered CTA, move purely decorative elements (the prompt cards) to the sides and give them a gradient.
rules.why: The cards are really for decoration anyway; this was the change that finished the CTA after the centered layout.
rules.evidence: move these to the side since they're really for decoration anyways

decisions.question: What should the hero call to action be on an AI product landing page?

options.name: Plain button
options.effect: A standard click-through; the author finds it less engaging and less cool-looking.

options.name: Typeable search or prompt bar
options.effect: Visitors start typing, which redirects them to log in; they are already engaged in an action. Mesh gradients go where a search icon could have been.
options.when: When the product itself is a prompt or search box, as with an AI chatbot.

decisions.recommendation: Typeable search bar: the user is already engaged in an action and more likely to see it through, and it looks cooler than a plain button.
decisions.evidence: for the header I think open AI has the right idea to have a search bar

decisions.question: How do you add attention to a clean hero section?

options.name: Background shapes
options.effect: Looked messy against Google's typically clean style.

options.name: Product-native animation (chatbot thinking loader at the bottom of the header)
options.effect: Looks like the AI is actually thinking; an eye-catching animation.
options.when: When the product has a recognisable loading or working state.

decisions.recommendation: The chatbot loading animation, because background shapes looked messy.
decisions.evidence: I tried background shapes but those looked messy

decisions.question: Where should gradients be used on an AI product site?

options.name: Mesh gradient on the hero search bar
options.effect: Signals AI; mesh gradients are called synonymous with AI.

options.name: Darkened two-color gradient as the dark-mode background
options.effect: Adds subtle color to a dark page using the brand's primary colors.

options.name: Gradient stroke on the purchase card and on hover
options.effect: Highlights the CTA card and adds brand color on interaction.
options.when: For the plan you want people to pick, and hover states.

options.name: Gradient icons
options.effect: The author did not like them and switched to solid Google blue.

decisions.recommendation: Use gradients on the hero, backgrounds, CTA strokes and hover strokes, but not on icons.
decisions.evidence: start overusing some mesh gradi; we can apply this gradient stroke; switch that to a nice Google blue

decisions.question: Which layout should a marketing feature or showcase section use?

options.name: Bento layout
options.effect: Cards with headers, short descriptions and integrated diagrams or product UI.
options.when: Features section with several distinct capabilities.

options.name: Text on the left, image on the right
options.effect: The author calls it the lame default.
options.when: Fallback when a fancier layout does not fit the content.

options.name: Multi-image showcase borrowed from the Chrome site
options.effect: Several images (a fourth added) with chatbot elements so it feels like a real chatbot.
options.when: Showing off image generation or visual output.

options.name: Layout that breaks the box by extending off the page
options.effect: Cards run off the edge of the page, with navigation to move through them.
options.when: An explore or browse section with many items.

decisions.recommendation: Bento for features, the Chrome-style showcase for images, and the off-page layout for exploring; the first image layout was dropped because it did not leave enough room for the content.
decisions.evidence: a good time to jump on the bandwagon of creating a Bento layout

decisions.question: How should image cards respond on hover?

options.name: Zoom-in effect
options.effect: A zoom-in effect the author loves on the Chrome website; it gave him the idea of a hover-driven section.
options.when: The starting idea for a hover-driven section.

options.name: Blur, enlarge and reveal text
options.effect: The image blurs and grows while additional text pops up; a classy interactive effect.
options.when: When cards need to hold more information than fits at rest.

decisions.recommendation: Blur the image, make it larger and pop up additional text (the Accenture-style effect).
decisions.evidence: on Hover we blur the image make it larger and pop up some additional text

decisions.question: Where should a rarely needed plan (Enterprise) go?

options.name: Its own section or card
options.effect: Takes space for information most visitors do not need.

options.name: A tiny button on every plan
options.effect: Keeps the plans compact while still offering the path.
options.when: When the option is irrelevant to most visitors.

decisions.recommendation: A tiny button on all the plans, because the Enterprise part is not useful for about 98% of visitors.
decisions.evidence: this isn't useful for like 98% of people passing through

decisions.question: How should the final call-to-action section be laid out?

options.name: Prompt cards with a typeable card at the bottom
options.effect: Felt weird.

options.name: Typeable card just below the text
options.effect: The spacing did not feel right.

options.name: Card collapsed into just the search bar
options.effect: Still did not feel right.

options.name: Centered layout
options.effect: Better.

options.name: Centered search bar with the prompt cards moved to the sides as gradient decoration
options.effect: The final version; the cards are there for decoration.

decisions.recommendation: Centered layout with the decorative prompt cards moved to the side and given a gradient, echoing the search bar from the header.
decisions.evidence: I went through about four different layouts before arriving on one I liked

decisions.question: What visual should carry a privacy section?

options.name: Lock icon
options.effect: Feels more like Apple.

options.name: Shield icon
options.effect: Feels more like Google.

options.name: Grid with isometrics and blue concentric circles
options.effect: Replaced a result the author thought looked lame; adds more visual interest.
options.when: When the plain icon treatment looks lame.

decisions.recommendation: The shield for brand fit, then a grid with isometrics and blue concentric circles to make it better.
decisions.evidence: the shield seems more like Google whereas I think Apple generally uses the lock icon

process.step: Audit the current and competitor sites
process.detail: Look at OpenAI, Microsoft, Midjourney, Gemini and the Chrome landing page and note what is weak (lopsided layout, too many tabs and videos, neglected page) and what works.
Pull from Microsoft Copilot, OpenAI, Google Chrome and other Google products.
Choose mesh gradients, a healthy dose of noise and fully rounded corners.
Draft the section order (partly generated with Gemini, loosely following Microsoft's landing page) so three separate Google pages condense into one.
Typeable search bar CTA with a mesh gradient, a punchy headline, the Google logo on a white background and the Gemini star, plus the chatbot loading animation for attention.

process.step: Build each section by borrowing and adapting
process.detail: Bento features with product UI and diagrams, an image showcase, merged plans with hover effects, an explore section, privacy, CTA, blog and footer.
Scroll through overlapping pages and keep only the key points (cost, better AI, document uploads).
Try multiple layouts for a section (about four for the CTA) and keep adjusting until spacing and balance feel right.
If a layout is already used on the page, choose another for the next section.

process.step: Close with a footer that mirrors the header
process.detail: Base the footer on the Gemini website's header and use the same element as the page header, swapping the Google logo for the Gemini one.

caveats: Published July 2024; the critiques of OpenAI, Microsoft and Gemini sites describe those sites at that time.
The author says the finished design is entirely not mobile optimized.
Self-promotion: the Figma file is offered as a free download via the description link (kolejain.com/resource), plus a subscribe plug.
Mostly opinion: the claim that a search bar makes users more likely to follow through, and the 98% figure, are stated without data.
The author openly 'steals' layouts and effects from Chrome, OpenAI, Accenture and Gemini; OpenDesigner treats references as structure, not identity [inferred].
No media list was available, so visual notes come from the narration only.

Auto-caption errors corrected where certain: 'RO map' is roadmap, 'I advaned' is Gemini Advanced, 'Flat icon' is Flaticon, 'stock' is stuck, 'gradi in action' is gradients in action; 'Chrome has a bump and landing page' is unclear.
